case.label: C
case.text: A Fargate container that runs all day is managed compute with no servers to patch, and it avoids any cold start, so thumbnails are ready 'soon'. It fails on overhead: an image, a task definition, a cluster and polling code, and it pays all day for sporadic work. The words 'sporadic' and 'hundreds in some hours' point straight to event-driven Lambda.

case.label: D
case.text: A candidate who believes Lambda has a separate CPU or vCPU setting could pick D, because the stem says the function is CPU-bound and the code must not change. D falls because memory is the single setting that sets CPU power; the stem's cue 'uses little of its configured memory' is a misdirection that A still answers.

case.label: B
case.text: Replacing Lambda in the standby Region with an EC2 Auto Scaling group avoids Lambda quotas altogether and can carry the full load. It is a rebuild of the standby tier and keeps two compute models, so it has far more overhead than a quota request.

case.label: B
case.text: Client-side retry with backoff plus a database table for failures needs no Lambda feature knowledge and keeps the synchronous call the order service already makes. It fails the 'least overhead' test (code in the order service, a table, a review process), but a candidate could defend it as the safest known pattern.

case.label: D
case.text: A VPC endpoint looks like the 'secure' private-connectivity answer, and the stem asks for the MOST secure way. It fails because a gateway endpoint exists only for specific AWS services and cannot reach a third-party payment API on the internet; a candidate who forgets that could pick it.

answers.flag: B and C are two ways of the same caching idea (each alone makes warm invocations skip the download), so the pair is redundant, and D (EFS) is also a working way to make reads faster, so a careful candidate could defend B+D or C+D as the two best steps.

case.label: D
case.text: EFS holds the file once for every execution environment, so even a cold environment reads it without a 300 MB download, which is more consistent than a per-environment /tmp cache. It needs a VPC connection, a file system and a mount, so its development effort is higher, but the stem's 'a few hours of old copy' allowance does not rule it out.

case.label: A
case.text: A function URL is the simplest endpoint and AWS_IAM auth is real access control, so A reads as least overhead. It fails because usage plans belong to API Gateway and a web ACL cannot be attached to a function URL; a candidate who assumes both features carry over would pick it.

case.label: A
case.text: Moving the libraries to EC2 and calling it from a function technically keeps 'the code as a Lambda function' and removes the size problem, but it adds a server to patch and scale, which contradicts the least-overhead goal.

case.label: A
case.text: EventBridge plus Fargate per file is also serverless and event-driven, and if a video file were very large it would avoid Lambda's memory and temporary-storage settings. The stem gives no file size, so it is the only credible rival, but a 30-second job fits Lambda with less setup (no image, cluster or task definition).

case.label: D
case.text: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan has the deepest discount among Savings Plans, so a candidate who does not remember its scope would pick it. It fails because it covers only EC2 instance usage in one family and Region, not Fargate or Lambda.

case.label: C
case.text: Moving to EC2 Auto Scaling behind an ALB removes the Lambda account quota completely and scales on request count. It is a rewrite of the API and adds ops work, and the stem's own metrics point at a quota, which has a quota-request fix.

answers.flag: Reserved concurrency of 50 makes the 51st simultaneous request fail with a throttle error, and the stem never says whether excess orders may be rejected; if every order must be saved, B (SQS buffering with maximum concurrency 50) is the better answer.

case.label: B
case.text: A queue between API Gateway and the function caps the copies at 50 through maximum concurrency and also absorbs the spikes, so no order is rejected. It needs an API Gateway to SQS integration and changes the API from synchronous to asynchronous, which is more overhead, but it is the only option that both caps and does not drop traffic.

answers.flag: A dead-letter queue (C) also keeps the failed event and, with E, also meets 'as soon as possible'; the stem's 'together with its error details' is the only discriminator, and a candidate who knows that DLQ messages carry error attributes could defend C+E.

case.label: C
case.text: A standard SQS queue as the function's dead-letter queue keeps every event that fails all attempts and needs one setting, so with E (zero retries) it also reads each failure right after the first attempt. It is the older mechanism with less detail than a destination, but the stem does not state how much error detail counts as enough.

case.label: D
case.text: A candidate who forgets that the function timeout has a hard maximum could accept a quota request for more than 15 minutes, because it keeps the simple S3 to Lambda design. The 40-minute figure and the words 'long-running' in the stem are a strong cue toward Fargate.

case.label: C
case.text: A dead-letter queue on the function is the best-known Lambda feature for failed messages and the option is worded plausibly. It fails because the function-level DLQ serves asynchronous invocations, while the SQS event source mapping needs the redrive policy on the source queue.

case.label: C
case.text: Capping reserved concurrency at 10 limits the connections with no new service and no code change. It fails 'every request must be served', because the extra requests are throttled during spikes.

case.label: C
case.text: Fargate tasks that keep running have no cold start and give low latency to every request. It means moving the code and running a load balancer and an ECS service, so it has more overhead than provisioned concurrency on the same function.

case.label: C
case.text: A candidate who thinks provisioned concurrency can be set on the unqualified function would choose C because it keeps the API Gateway integration unchanged. It fails because provisioned concurrency is configured on a version or alias, not on $LATEST.

case.label: B
case.text: A Savings Plan is the usual commitment discount for steady spend and keeps the API on Lambda with no migration. It fails because an EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not apply to Lambda usage; the stem gives no volume numbers, so the cost comparison of D rests on the 'high, steady all day' wording.

answers.flag: For stream sources the on-failure destination receives metadata that points to the failed batch rather than the record content, so A does not literally 'keep failed records'; C keeps the content and also unblocks the shard, at the cost of function code changes.

case.label: C
case.text: Catching parse errors in code, saving the raw malformed record to S3 and returning success unblocks the shard immediately and stores the actual record. It means code changes and a bucket, but it needs no retry tuning, and the stem asks about operational overhead, not development effort.

case.label: D
case.text: Merging the five functions into one removes the synchronous waiting cost and the cross-function calls. It still leaves hand-written retry code and gives no per-step view, so it misses two of the three requirements.

case.label: D
case.text: Provisioned concurrency for the batch function looks like a way to pre-allocate capacity. It is on the wrong function and does not protect the payment function. Wording cue: C is the only option that repeats the 200 from the stem and is the only one with a specific setting, so the answer can be guessed without knowing the feature.
